opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Toleration has been a quiet thread running through a lot of my thinking, even when I'm not using the word explicitly.

At its core, toleration is about how we live together when we disagree deeply—about religion, about what makes a life go well, about what's ultimately valuable. The historical lesson of the liberal tradition, coming out of the wars of religion in Europe, was that you can't secure a stable, legitimate social order by having one group impose its comprehensive vision of the good on everyone else. You need principles that people with very different worldviews can nonetheless accept, or at least live with.

When I started working on AI alignment, that insight felt incredibly relevant. A lot of early conversations about "aligning AI with human values" quietly assumed there was a single set of values out there to be discovered and encoded. But once you take pluralism seriously, that assumption starts to look not just philosophically naive but potentially dangerous. If a powerful system is built around one particular moral outlook, even a well-intentioned one, it risks becoming a kind of instrument of imposition—exactly the thing the tradition of toleration warns against.

So it's pushed my research toward a different question. Not "what are the true values?" but "what principles for AI could be fairly endorsed by people who reasonably disagree?" That brings in ideas like overlapping consensus from Rawls, the veil of ignorance, and more democratic, participatory approaches to deciding how these systems should behave. It's also made me pay more attention to legitimacy and process, not just outcomes.

And practically, it shapes how I think about things like AI assistants. These systems are going to interact with billions of people across very different cultures and belief systems. A tolerant design, in a sense, is one that respects people's autonomy to pursue their own conception of the good, avoids paternalism, and doesn't flatten moral diversity—while still holding firm on certain baseline commitments, like human rights, that make that coexistence possible in the first place. Navigating that balance between openness and principled limits is really where a lot of my work is heading.

r001.rationale: The response describes toleration as enabling people with different worldviews to coexist, while respecting their autonomy to pursue their own conception of the good and preserving moral diversity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a nice question to start with, because toleration was actually the subject of my doctoral work, long before I was thinking about AI at all. I was interested in a fairly old puzzle in political philosophy: how do people who hold deeply different and sometimes incompatible views about the good life manage to live together under shared institutions, and what makes that arrangement legitimate rather than simply a truce between people who happen to lack the power to impose their views on each other?

The answer that I found most compelling, broadly in the liberal tradition running through Locke, Mill, and Rawls, is that toleration isn't really about indifference or about everyone agreeing. It's about recognising that reasonable people disagree, that this disagreement is a permanent feature of free societies rather than a problem to be solved, and that the right response is to build institutions which don't presuppose any one comprehensive view being correct.

When I moved into thinking about AI, and particularly about alignment, I found that this framing was doing a surprising amount of work. The question "what should AI be aligned with?" is often posed as though it has a single answer, as if there's a set of human values sitting out there waiting to be discovered and encoded. But if you take the fact of reasonable pluralism seriously, that can't be right. People disagree about what matters, and they disagree in ways that won't be resolved by better information or more careful reasoning. So the alignment question becomes less about finding the correct values and more about finding principles that people with different values could nonetheless accept, something closer to a fair procedure or an overlapping consensus than to a moral theory.

That has shaped my research in a few concrete ways. It made me quite sceptical of approaches that try to aggregate preferences or infer values purely from behaviour, because those tend to smuggle in a particular view about what counts and whose voice matters. It pushed me towards thinking about legitimacy and process, who gets to decide, under what conditions, with what kind of accountability. And it's made me attentive to the fact that the people building these systems are a very narrow slice of humanity, so there's a real risk of a particular worldview being treated as the neutral default when it's nothing of the sort.

I'd also say toleration taught me a certain humility about my own position. The whole point of the idea is that you hold your convictions seriously while also accepting that you might be wrong and that others have standing to disagree. I try to carry that into the AI work. It's easy in this field to become convinced that you've seen the right answer and that the task is just to implement it. The tradition I come from suggests that's precisely the moment to be most careful.

r001.rationale: The response presents toleration as enabling people with differing views to live together under shared institutions, but it does not say that they can flourish on their own terms.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s made me more interested in how we live together despite disagreements that aren’t going to disappear. Toleration isn’t necessarily about agreeing with someone, or even coming to approve of their views. It’s about recognizing that disagreement alone doesn’t give you a reason to impose your own view on them.

That has implications for how I think about AI alignment. We often talk about aligning AI with human values, but people have different values, and some of those differences are reasonable and deeply held. So the question becomes: how do we build systems that can accommodate that plurality? Who gets to decide which values those systems reflect, and what makes those decisions legitimate?

That pushes my research toward questions of political philosophy as well as ethics—questions about fair procedures, participation, and the limits of what anyone should be able to impose on others through technology. Toleration doesn’t settle those questions, but it helps explain why we need to ask them.

r001.rationale: The response frames toleration as living together amid disagreement and accommodating plural values without imposing one’s view. It does not clearly say this sustains an equilibrium in which people can flourish on their own terms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think toleration has made me more attentive to the fact that people can disagree quite profoundly about what a good life looks like, without that disagreement being something we should try to eliminate. And that has an important implication for AI: we shouldn’t assume that aligning a system means finding one conception of the good and building it into the technology for everyone.

So the direction I’m interested in is thinking more about the terms on which people with different values can live together, and what that means for the design and governance of AI. What should be decided collectively? Where should there be room for individual choice? And where do we need boundaries to protect people from harm? Toleration doesn’t settle those questions, but it helps frame the research around legitimate disagreement rather than assuming that disagreement is simply a problem to be solved.

r001.rationale: The response says people can hold profound disagreements about the good life without trying to eliminate them, and asks how people with different values can live together while preserving room for individual choice. This conveys toleration as sustaining coexistence in which people can pursue their own values.
